narr.Muddle Through:
Status-quo extension of the post-demerger franchise: mining-customer demand holds, input costs are broadly stable, and the US cost-curve advantage from long-term gas contracts is intact in the near term. The single most consequential firm-specific variable — the US gas-contract roll-off in the 2028–2030 window — is built explicitly into the margin path (−50/−100/−150 bps cumulative Y3/Y4/Y5), and is offset by peer-gap closure toward Orica-level efficiency.

Why AUD 3.07? It sits below market (AUD 3.61, ~15%) — on a Muddle Through path the framework reads consensus as somewhat rich at the centre, but the emphasis is the scenario asymmetry around this point rather than the central level.

Mental short-cut: a cyclical industrial priced fairly at the centre, but with a downside that bites ~4.2× harder than the upside lifts.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Mining capex healthy, transition-mineral demand (copper, lithium, nickel) pulls volumes, and a modest margin lift comes through. The upside is real but capped by the oligopolistic structure — +AUD 0.49 above Muddle Through.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Close to neutral. A modest labour-cost benefit on SG&A from automation, otherwise the macro is broadly status-quo. −3% vs Muddle Through — the least-sensitive scenario.
narr.Fragmentation: DNL sits ~90% in the US-aligned bloc (USA + Australia), which is the slower-growing bloc; cross-bloc ammonium-nitrate and ammonia flows are regulatorily sensitive and supply chains duplicate. Partially offset by Australia’s strategic-mineral position. −28%.
narr.Disorderly Climate: Coal customers (~35% of the mix) attrit faster than the standard fade assumes; carbon costs flow through ammonia into bulk ANFO; capex rises. A partial offset from transition-mineral mining demand. The moat decays over a shortened fade (§10.6). −62%.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The binding downside. Sustained input-cost inflation that cannot be passed through — supplier power blocks it while mining customers resist price increases — combined with slowing mining capex. −67% vs Muddle Through; the −AUD 2.05 that sets the 4.2× asymmetry.

_forces.intro:
The industry. Industrial explosives is a mature, concentrated oligopoly — the top three (Orica, Dyno Nobel, MAXAM) hold ~65% of global volume and Australia is a duopoly. Scale incumbents earn moderate excess returns from long-term offtake contracts, on-site infrastructure and technology, while marginal players are pushed toward cost-of-capital returns; a profile weighted to high buyer power and high rivalry caps how durable those returns are.

Below, how Dyno Nobel sits within that archetype, force by force — industry rating is the archetype baseline, the badge is DNL’s position, and impact is the growth/margin offset.
rows: Mining-customer concentration is the binding constraint — top 3–5 global miners drive volume, are highly price-sensitive on bulk ANFO, and hold a real backward-integration threat.
Same mining-major customer mix as Orica
Anhydrous ammonia (and upstream natural gas) is the dominant input — contained for producers with long-term gas contracts, significant for spot-gas-exposed players.
Long-term US gas contracts shield ~70% of US gas through 2028; rolls off by FY31
Strong barriers — explosives licensing, dangerous-goods and environmental regulation, capital-intensive plants, and incumbents’ long-term offtake contracts and on-site infrastructure.
DNL is itself the new entrant via the DNEL ramp in emerging markets
No meaningful substitute for industrial explosives in hard-rock mining; mechanical excavation is niche — coal-volume decline is a demand question, not a substitute one.
Intra-industry tech substitution affects all players equally
Concentrated global oligopoly (Orica / Dyno Nobel / MAXAM ~65%); Australia a duopoly. Bulk ANFO competes on price while technology products differentiate.
#2 vs Orica #1; more bulk-ANFO, fewer high-margin electronic detonators
_forces.net: −25 bps net growth offset (rivalry −30 + product-mix −10 + new-entrants +15). The supplier-power margin edge is transitory — it rolls off with the gas contracts.

dnl._position:
Franchise & moat
  • Pure-play post-demerger – explosives-only after the March 2025 Incitec Pivot split (fertilisers demerged, entity renamed); single reporting segment.
  • Global #2, Australian duopolist – #1 in North American industrial explosives (~30% share), #2 to Orica in Australia (~40% share), plus a sub-scale ~5% RoW book slowly gaining.
  • US cost-curve edge – transitory – long-term gas contracts put US ops in the bottom cost-curve quartile (~+200bps margin), rolling off through a 2028–2030 re-pricing window (6-year average maturity) to nil by FY31.
  • Switching-cost moat – 200+ on-site mobile manufacturing units at customer mine sites, multi-decade relationships and 5–10-year offtake contracts (BHP, Rio Tinto, FMG); ~78% of revenue contracted.
Geography, product & peers
  • Geography & currency – ~55% USA, ~35% Australia, ~10% RoW; per-entity functional currency under IAS 21 (parent AUD, Dyno Nobel Americas USD-functional on US revenue, gas and ammonia).
  • Product & customer mix – ~50% commodity bulk ANFO, ~18% higher-growth electronic detonators (DigiShot); ~35% coal-exposed, offset by transition-mineral demand. Top 5 customers ~45% of revenue.
  • Peer-gap to Orica – Orica is ~30% larger with a technology and diversification lead, driving a net ~25bps company-position growth drag (−30 rivalry, −10 mix, +15 EM ramp).
Financials & risks
  • Balance sheet – net debt/EBITDA 2.12x; AUD 647m liquidity; thin FY25 free cash flow (AUD 101m) vs AUD 162m dividends + AUD 289m buybacks; 60–70% payout target.
  • Key risks – gas/ammonia input costs, coal-customer transition, and a weak large-project execution record (Louisiana ammonia overruns 2017–2020); carbon exposure rated high given ~55% ammonia self-supply.

worldDesc.Muddle Through:
Post-2022 friction proves persistent rather than transitional: inflation cools but lands above target (2.5–3.5%) and central banks tacitly accept the overshoot rather than crush demand. Real rates settle structurally higher than the 2010s (~1.0%). The US keeps outperforming on fiscal expansion, AI investment and immigration, but the lift doesn’t propagate to Europe or EM. Climate policy stays patchy and AI’s productivity transmission is slow, with rents concentrating in platform owners. No crisis, no resolution — a grinding extension of present conditions. Global growth ~2.3%.

Macro picture. Global growth ~2.3% (US ~2.4% leads; advanced-economy aggregate 1.5–2.0%; EM bifurcating by commodity exposure). Headline inflation settles ~3.0% — above target but tacitly accepted rather than fought; real policy rates ~1.0%, materially above the 2010s zero-bound. USD firm but range-bound.

What would move the world elsewhere. Sustained inflation re-anchoring at target → Orderly Convergence; expectations breaking above 3% with second-round wage dynamics → Stagflation Persists; any regime-changing shock in energy, markets, climate or geopolitics → one of the boundary scenarios.
worldDesc.Orderly Convergence:
The conditions for benign resolution stack up at once. Supply-side normalisation plus genuine AI productivity gains absorb wage pressure, so inflation returns to ~2.3% without a demand crush; real rates settle modestly positive. The political reset climate policy needed happens, and geopolitical tensions materially de-escalate. This time US growth propagates — pulling Europe out of stagnation and supporting EM — and AI rents diffuse, re-expanding growth multiples. Global growth recovers to 3.0–3.2%.

Macro picture. Growth recovers to 3.0–3.2% (US 2.5%; Europe out of stagnation to 1.8–2.2%; EM 4–5%). Advanced-economy inflation back to ~2.3% by year 3; real policy rates a modestly positive ~0.8%. The USD softens as the Fed eases and capital flows reglobalise.

What would move the world elsewhere. Sticky inflation despite supply normalisation → Muddle Through; expectations un-anchoring → Stagflation Persists; geopolitical escalation → Fragmentation; a physical-loss or carbon-policy crisis → Disorderly Climate; a persistent enterprise-AI adoption lag → AI Productivity Lag.
worldDesc.Stagflation Persists:
The IMF severe scenario plays out: an energy shock spikes prices and keeps them elevated, inflation expectations break above the 3% credibility threshold, and second-round wage-price dynamics take hold. Central banks lose credibility and hold restrictive policy through the horizon; real rates settle 2–3% with recession inside the scenario. Climate policy backslides as a cost-of-living crisis crushes the transition coalition; growth-stock multiples compress and trade barriers ratchet up. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0%.

Macro picture. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0% with an in-scenario recession (advanced economies contract ~0.5% in year 2). Inflation peaks 5.5–6% then settles 4–5%; nominal cash rates 5–7%, real rates ~2.5%. USD strong on rate-differential and safe-haven flows, with some EM currency crises.

What would move the world elsewhere. The energy spike fading without second-round transmission, or credible central-bank re-anchoring → Muddle Through or Orderly Convergence; a deeper recession with rapid disinflation → a deflationary case outside the current set.
worldDesc.Fragmentation:
The US-China contest hardens and trade-as-weapon (tariffs, sanctions, export controls) becomes routine, extending into industrial and commodity flows. Supply chains regionalise into duplicated US-aligned and China-aligned systems, energy markets bifurcate, and critical-minerals access becomes the new geopolitical front. The duplicated footprint is inflationary (~3.5%) and growth bifurcates — China-aligned economies may outpace the US-aligned bloc, with Europe hit hardest and Australia facing an acute security-vs-supply dilemma. The new equilibrium is structurally inferior.

Macro picture. Growth ~2.0%, below Muddle Through on supply-chain-duplication costs and bifurcated by bloc (China-aligned 3.5–4.0%; US-aligned ~1.8%). Advanced-economy inflation ~3.5%; real rates ~1.5%. USD reserve share erodes gradually but stays dominant; gold prominent as a cross-bloc settlement medium.

What would move the world elsewhere. Major diplomatic breakthroughs — a substantive US-China trade framework, a Russia-Ukraine settlement, an Iran deal revival — would weaken the bloc-formation logic; sustained globalisation gains in low-sensitivity categories would signal barrier-stability rather than ratcheting.
worldDesc.Disorderly Climate:
The already-running disorderly climate path has its crystallisation moment — most likely a confluence of a catastrophic insured-loss event, regulator-forced de-leveraging of carbon-intensive loan books, and a carbon-price spike. Policy snaps from drift to abrupt crisis action: carbon prices to EUR 200+, border-adjustment mechanisms, expanded transition subsidies. Capital reallocates abruptly, so sectoral dispersion widens sharply even as aggregate growth stays near Muddle Through (~2.0–2.2%, inflation 4.5–5% from carbon pass-through). This scenario tests terminal-state convergence hardest — assumed-perpetual moats reveal stranded-asset half-lives inside the horizon.

Macro picture. Aggregate growth 2.0–2.2% (near Muddle Through) but with far wider sectoral dispersion. Inflation peaks 4.5–5% from carbon-cost pass-through before easing to ~3% by year 10; real rates ~1.5% with elevated volatility. The EU ETS carbon price spikes to EUR 200+ and settles ~EUR 200–220; insurance is repriced sharply in physical-risk regions.

What would move the world elsewhere. Continued drift without crystallisation → Muddle Through; a political reset enabling orderly transition → Orderly Convergence; climate-policy backsliding under a macro crisis → Stagflation’s climate-stagnant posture.
worldDesc.AI Productivity Lag:
The Solow paradox at AI scale. Capability and capex advance genuinely (deficit-funded, US-led), but economy-wide productivity transformation doesn’t arrive on the bull timeline: enterprise adoption is slow, so aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5% versus the 1.5%+ current investment implies. Rents capture is asymmetric — platform owners take the bulk while broad enterprise pays without proportional payback — and market concentration intensifies. The saving grace is the labour-cost channel: AI contains white-collar wage growth even where productivity transmission is weak. Headline numbers resemble Muddle Through, but the underlying story differs.

Macro picture. Growth 1.9–2.0%, modestly below Muddle Through; inflation ~3.0% and real rates ~1.0% — both Muddle-Through-like. Aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5%. The tell: headline numbers resemble Muddle Through while the story underneath is fundamentally different.

What would move the world elsewhere. Enterprise-AI adoption broadening with genuine TFP flow-through → Orderly Convergence; an AI-capex collapse or financial-market unwind → a tech-investment-unwind stress variant outside the set; a major non-AI shock → Stagflation, Fragmentation or Disorderly Climate depending on the shock.

_drtheory: Risk-free rate

The theoretically correct rate is a zero-coupon (spot) sovereign yield in the cash-flow currency, matched to the timing of each cash flow — a coupon bond’s yield-to-maturity blends reinvestment assumptions across its life and is only an average. In practice the deep, liquid 10-year benchmark is used as a proxy, with longer tenors for very long-life assets; a steeply sloped curve is where that approximation most distorts long-dated NPVs.
10-year Commonwealth Government Securities YTM, 4.30% (indicative, May 2026). Single spot 10-year — the pragmatic-benchmark choice, no duration-matching or normalisation.
Equity risk premium

The expected excess return of equities over the risk-free asset. It is unobservable, so it is estimated from long-run historical premia, forward-looking/implied models, or surveys — none decisive. Mature-market estimates cluster around 5–6%, but the statistical error is wide, so the figure is best treated as a reasoned convention rather than a measurement.
5.0% — a Damodaran-style mature-Australia premium, deliberately ~100bps below the 6.0% Australian-expert convention, with a small country premium baked in.
Beta

A single-stock regression beta is noisy and shifts with the estimation window and the index chosen, so triangulate from a comparable set: unlever peer equity betas to asset betas and re-lever to the subject’s target capital structure, cross-checked against adjusted (mean-reverting) or fundamental betas. Index choice — local versus global — matters most when a company’s earnings currency differs from its listing.
Peer triangulation, rejecting the measured 0.36 (unreliable post-demerger): Orica ~1.05 / Yara ~1.20 / ICL ~1.10 cluster (Sasol 1.45 excluded) → selected 1.10.
Cost of debt

The risk-free rate plus a credit-spread margin set by the company’s (or its comparable set’s) target credit rating, referencing traded corporate-bond spreads over sovereigns at matching tenor. Use a through-the-cycle target rating consistent with the assumed gearing, not the current coupon.
6.00% pre-tax = an AUD investment-grade BBB-tier spread (~170bps) over the 10-year sovereign; after-tax 6.00% × (1−0.30) = 4.20%.
Gearing / capital-structure weights

Weight equity and debt at market value on a target, through-the-cycle basis — informed by the subject’s own structure and the comparable-set average rather than a single spot snapshot, which is volatile and often inconsistent with the betas measured over the same window.
Market-value weights E/V 83.5% / D/V 16.5% (equity = 1,770m shares × AUD 3.61 ≈ 6,390; debt = net debt 1,261 at the 31 Mar 2026 anchor, §5.3). Market-value basis.
WACC vs cost of equity

For an ordinary company, discount ungeared after-tax cash flows (FCFF) at the WACC and bridge enterprise value to equity via net debt. For a bank, funding — deposits and wholesale debt — is an operating input rather than financing, so discount cash flows to equity at the cost of equity directly; a WACC/EV bridge would be wrong.
WACC ≈ 8.88% (Re 9.80% at β 1.10; 83.5% equity + 16.5% debt at 4.20% after-tax). Held constant across scenarios (§3.5).

narr.Muddle Through:
Status-quo extension: NIM held at the through-cycle 1.94% anchor, the UNITE cost-to-income glide delivers part of the peer-gap closure, and credit losses run at the 18 bps through-cycle anchor. CET1 (12.42%) sits comfortably above target, supporting the buyback.

Why AUD 30.15, ~15% below market? The market (AUD 35.32) is implicitly trading WBC at a successful-transformation outcome — essentially the Orderly Convergence scenario (AUD 35.46) — not at this status-quo base. To converge to market on a Muddle Through path, terminal ROE has to be 12.1% (CBA-like), not the archetype mid-point.

Mental short-cut: the market is paying for the transformation; Muddle Through is what you get if it only half-lands.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Healthy loan growth, a benign credit cycle and modest NIM uplift; UNITE closes most of the cost-to-income gap. At AUD 35.46 it sits essentially at market — the framework’s read on what current pricing implies. +17.6% vs Muddle Through.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Close to neutral. A modest cost benefit from automation, offset by weaker macro loan demand. −1.3% vs Muddle Through.
narr.Fragmentation: Hits non-interest income (markets / institutional) more than net interest income, with modest credit losses on the business book. −9.5%.
narr.Disorderly Climate: APRA climate-adjusted RWA models lift capital intensity for vulnerable zones; WBC’s #2 mortgage book carries more absolute climate-vulnerable exposure than NAB or ANZ. Transmission is mainly via terminal-ROE compression (−1.5pp). −23%.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The binding downside. NIM compresses −20 bps (deposit competition + slow front-book repricing), credit losses lift to peak-cycle (+50 bps), and cost growth runs ahead of the glide. CET1 forces payout from 75% down to ~50% to rebuild capital. NPAT Y5 AUD 3.7bn vs MT AUD 8.9bn. −33%.

_forces.intro:
The industry. The Australian majors are a durable, APRA-protected oligopoly — four-pillars policy, D-SIB capital floors and deep deposit franchises keep the Big Four insulated on a 5–10 year view. Roughly 55% of the pool is Australian housing, where the tension between competitive front-book pricing and sticky back-book margin is the single most important profitability dynamic; returns are structurally solid but rate- and credit-cycle sensitive.

Below, how Westpac sits within that archetype, force by force — industry rating is the archetype baseline, the badge is WBC’s position, and impact is the NIM/growth offset.
rows: Retail customers have low switching propensity (relationship inertia, bundling, discharge friction); the binding constraint sits in the marginal front-book mortgage-refinancing cohort.
Switching costs + oligopoly; standard across the Big Four
Deposit-holders and wholesale-debt investors are the funding ‘suppliers’ with real switching options, but the Big Four are price-takers within a narrow oligopolistic funding-cost range.
AUD 149bn non-interest-bearing transaction deposits — a funding-cost floor
APRA licensing, D-SIB capital floors (~11.5% CET1), distribution scale, and incumbent deposit-franchise funding advantage; neo-bank waves produced no material disruption.
Four-pillars policy + capital and licensing barriers

worldDesc.Muddle Through:
Post-2022 friction proves persistent rather than transitional: inflation cools but lands above target (2.5–3.5%) and central banks tacitly accept the overshoot rather than crush demand. Real rates settle structurally higher than the 2010s (~1.0%). The US keeps outperforming on fiscal expansion, AI investment and immigration, but the lift doesn’t propagate to Europe or EM. Climate policy stays patchy and AI’s productivity transmission is slow, with rents concentrating in platform owners. No crisis, no resolution — a grinding extension of present conditions. Global growth ~2.3%.

Macro picture. Global growth ~2.3% (US ~2.4% leads; advanced-economy aggregate 1.5–2.0%; EM bifurcating by commodity exposure). Headline inflation settles ~3.0% — above target but tacitly accepted rather than fought; real policy rates ~1.0%, materially above the 2010s zero-bound. USD firm but range-bound.

What would move the world elsewhere. Sustained inflation re-anchoring at target → Orderly Convergence; expectations breaking above 3% with second-round wage dynamics → Stagflation Persists; any regime-changing shock in energy, markets, climate or geopolitics → one of the boundary scenarios.
worldDesc.Orderly Convergence:
The conditions for benign resolution stack up at once. Supply-side normalisation plus genuine AI productivity gains absorb wage pressure, so inflation returns to ~2.3% without a demand crush; real rates settle modestly positive. The political reset climate policy needed happens, and geopolitical tensions materially de-escalate. This time US growth propagates — pulling Europe out of stagnation and supporting EM — and AI rents diffuse, re-expanding growth multiples. Global growth recovers to 3.0–3.2%.

Macro picture. Growth recovers to 3.0–3.2% (US 2.5%; Europe out of stagnation to 1.8–2.2%; EM 4–5%). Advanced-economy inflation back to ~2.3% by year 3; real policy rates a modestly positive ~0.8%. The USD softens as the Fed eases and capital flows reglobalise.

What would move the world elsewhere. Sticky inflation despite supply normalisation → Muddle Through; expectations un-anchoring → Stagflation Persists; geopolitical escalation → Fragmentation; a physical-loss or carbon-policy crisis → Disorderly Climate; a persistent enterprise-AI adoption lag → AI Productivity Lag.
worldDesc.Stagflation Persists:
The IMF severe scenario plays out: an energy shock spikes prices and keeps them elevated, inflation expectations break above the 3% credibility threshold, and second-round wage-price dynamics take hold. Central banks lose credibility and hold restrictive policy through the horizon; real rates settle 2–3% with recession inside the scenario. Climate policy backslides as a cost-of-living crisis crushes the transition coalition; growth-stock multiples compress and trade barriers ratchet up. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0%.

Macro picture. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0% with an in-scenario recession (advanced economies contract ~0.5% in year 2). Inflation peaks 5.5–6% then settles 4–5%; nominal cash rates 5–7%, real rates ~2.5%. USD strong on rate-differential and safe-haven flows, with some EM currency crises.

What would move the world elsewhere. The energy spike fading without second-round transmission, or credible central-bank re-anchoring → Muddle Through or Orderly Convergence; a deeper recession with rapid disinflation → a deflationary case outside the current set.
worldDesc.Fragmentation:
The US-China contest hardens and trade-as-weapon (tariffs, sanctions, export controls) becomes routine, extending into industrial and commodity flows. Supply chains regionalise into duplicated US-aligned and China-aligned systems, energy markets bifurcate, and critical-minerals access becomes the new geopolitical front. The duplicated footprint is inflationary (~3.5%) and growth bifurcates — China-aligned economies may outpace the US-aligned bloc, with Europe hit hardest and Australia facing an acute security-vs-supply dilemma. The new equilibrium is structurally inferior.

Macro picture. Growth ~2.0%, below Muddle Through on supply-chain-duplication costs and bifurcated by bloc (China-aligned 3.5–4.0%; US-aligned ~1.8%). Advanced-economy inflation ~3.5%; real rates ~1.5%. USD reserve share erodes gradually but stays dominant; gold prominent as a cross-bloc settlement medium.

What would move the world elsewhere. Major diplomatic breakthroughs — a substantive US-China trade framework, a Russia-Ukraine settlement, an Iran deal revival — would weaken the bloc-formation logic; sustained globalisation gains in low-sensitivity categories would signal barrier-stability rather than ratcheting.
worldDesc.Disorderly Climate:
The already-running disorderly climate path has its crystallisation moment — most likely a confluence of a catastrophic insured-loss event, regulator-forced de-leveraging of carbon-intensive loan books, and a carbon-price spike. Policy snaps from drift to abrupt crisis action: carbon prices to EUR 200+, border-adjustment mechanisms, expanded transition subsidies. Capital reallocates abruptly, so sectoral dispersion widens sharply even as aggregate growth stays near Muddle Through (~2.0–2.2%, inflation 4.5–5% from carbon pass-through). This scenario tests terminal-state convergence hardest — assumed-perpetual moats reveal stranded-asset half-lives inside the horizon.

Macro picture. Aggregate growth 2.0–2.2% (near Muddle Through) but with far wider sectoral dispersion. Inflation peaks 4.5–5% from carbon-cost pass-through before easing to ~3% by year 10; real rates ~1.5% with elevated volatility. The EU ETS carbon price spikes to EUR 200+ and settles ~EUR 200–220; insurance is repriced sharply in physical-risk regions.

What would move the world elsewhere. Continued drift without crystallisation → Muddle Through; a political reset enabling orderly transition → Orderly Convergence; climate-policy backsliding under a macro crisis → Stagflation’s climate-stagnant posture.
worldDesc.AI Productivity Lag:
The Solow paradox at AI scale. Capability and capex advance genuinely (deficit-funded, US-led), but economy-wide productivity transformation doesn’t arrive on the bull timeline: enterprise adoption is slow, so aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5% versus the 1.5%+ current investment implies. Rents capture is asymmetric — platform owners take the bulk while broad enterprise pays without proportional payback — and market concentration intensifies. The saving grace is the labour-cost channel: AI contains white-collar wage growth even where productivity transmission is weak. Headline numbers resemble Muddle Through, but the underlying story differs.

Macro picture. Growth 1.9–2.0%, modestly below Muddle Through; inflation ~3.0% and real rates ~1.0% — both Muddle-Through-like. Aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5%. The tell: headline numbers resemble Muddle Through while the story underneath is fundamentally different.

What would move the world elsewhere. Enterprise-AI adoption broadening with genuine TFP flow-through → Orderly Convergence; an AI-capex collapse or financial-market unwind → a tech-investment-unwind stress variant outside the set; a major non-AI shock → Stagflation, Fragmentation or Disorderly Climate depending on the shock.

_drtheory: Risk-free rate

The theoretically correct rate is a zero-coupon (spot) sovereign yield in the cash-flow currency, matched to the timing of each cash flow — a coupon bond’s yield-to-maturity blends reinvestment assumptions across its life and is only an average. In practice the deep, liquid 10-year benchmark is used as a proxy, with longer tenors for very long-life assets; a steeply sloped curve is where that approximation most distorts long-dated NPVs.
10-year Commonwealth Government Securities YTM, 4.30% (indicative, May 2026). Single spot 10-year — the pragmatic-benchmark choice.
Equity risk premium

The expected excess return of equities over the risk-free asset. It is unobservable, so it is estimated from long-run historical premia, forward-looking/implied models, or surveys — none decisive. Mature-market estimates cluster around 5–6%, but the statistical error is wide, so the figure is best treated as a reasoned convention rather than a measurement.
5.0% — a Damodaran-style mature-Australia premium, ~100bps below the 6.0% Australian-expert convention.
Beta

A single-stock regression beta is noisy and shifts with the estimation window and the index chosen, so triangulate from a comparable set: unlever peer equity betas to asset betas and re-lever to the subject’s target capital structure, cross-checked against adjusted (mean-reverting) or fundamental betas. Index choice — local versus global — matters most when a company’s earnings currency differs from its listing.
Peer triangulation: CBA 0.80 / NAB 0.72 / WBC 0.73 cluster → 0.75; ANZ 0.57 excluded as an institutional-dilution outlier, MQG 0.88 a different archetype. Measured 0.73 documented alongside.
Cost of debt

The risk-free rate plus a credit-spread margin set by the company’s (or its comparable set’s) target credit rating, referencing traded corporate-bond spreads over sovereigns at matching tenor. Use a through-the-cycle target rating consistent with the assumed gearing, not the current coupon.
Not applicable — a bank is discounted at cost of equity, with deposits and wholesale funding treated as operating inputs, not financing (§15).
Gearing / capital-structure weights

Weight equity and debt at market value on a target, through-the-cycle basis — informed by the subject’s own structure and the comparable-set average rather than a single spot snapshot, which is volatile and often inconsistent with the betas measured over the same window.
Not applicable — no WACC / EV bridge for a bank.
WACC vs cost of equity

For an ordinary company, discount ungeared after-tax cash flows (FCFF) at the WACC and bridge enterprise value to equity via net debt. For a bank, funding — deposits and wholesale debt — is an operating input rather than financing, so discount cash flows to equity at the cost of equity directly; a WACC/EV bridge would be wrong.
Cost of equity 8.05% (Rf 4.30% + β 0.75 × ERP 5.0%), held constant across scenarios, no WACC/EV bridge — the bank convention (§15).

narr.Muddle Through:
Post-2022 friction persists without crushing demand. The plasma franchise resumes its secular 5–7% Ig path once the near-term Behring trough (Medicare Part D redesign + China access soft patch) annualises across FY26–27. Vertical integration and fractionation scale hold the margin edge; peer-gap closure delivers +150 bps to Behring by FY31 (full +250 reserved for the upside). Terminal margin 30%, g 3%.

Why ~93% above market? Not because the cash-flow path is heroic — the near-term lines sit on top of consensus — but because the terminal capitalises a high-quality compounder at ~22× forward earnings while the market trades CSL at ~11×. The entire gap is a disagreement about the terminal, not the next two years. Per §16 this premium is a cause for curiosity, not a calibration error: the §3.5.7 reverse-DCF shows no single lever reconciles to market (it would need β ≈ 1.7, or a terminal margin ~half FY25’s, or perpetual −4% contraction), so β is deliberately held at 0.85 to keep the framework rules-based and the gap visible.

Mental short-cut: CSL is a margin story, not a volume story — in every scenario the plasma keeps flowing, so watch the gap between what CSL pays US donors and what Medicare lets it charge. The framework prices the recovery; the market prices the trough.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Inflation re-anchors, real rates normalise, and a productivity surprise eases costs. That buys CSL a faster Behring-trough exit and genuine donor-wage relief, making the full +250 bps peer-gap closure credible. Terminal margin 31.5%, g 3.25%. Instructive that the upside is only +16% — a defensive staple has no operating-leverage explosion; the upside is quiet compounding in a kind world.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Foundation models advance and gains concentrate in platform owners, showing up as white-collar wage containment — a mild tailwind on CSL’s ~USD 1bn G&A and USD 1.4bn R&D. But softer macro pulls terminal g to 2.875%. The two roughly offset — the tech axis barely touches a plasma franchise. −2.6% vs Muddle Through.
narr.Disorderly Climate: Disorderly transition; carbon-cost pass-through runs inflation 3–5%. CSL is exposed through cost, not demand: fractionation is energy-intensive and distribution is cold-chain dependent, so margins compress. The one genuine portfolio offset sits here — Seqirus pandemic / health-disruption optionality lifts vaccine demand — which is why this lands better than Fragmentation despite the larger cost shock. Terminal margin 28%. −14.2%.
narr.Fragmentation: Trade barriers harden, supply chains localise, and China access becomes a geopolitical instrument. CSL’s collect-in-US / fractionate / distribute-globally model is structurally awkward when blocs fragment, and Behring’s China Ig access is the most exposed line. Peer-gap closure stalls to zero and tax drifts to 20%. With no offsetting segment (unlike the Seqirus climate cushion), the channels compound. −17.4% — the second-worst.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The downside boundary and the clearest illustration of the thesis: plasma demand still holds, so the entire stress arrives as margin — US donor-collection wages surge (supplier-power channel at full stretch), payors press hard on price, and peer-gap closure reverses (Behring margin 150 bps below the FY25 base). Terminal margin 26.5%. Revenue is near-indistinguishable from Muddle Through; the whole 21% fall is the donor-vs-payor squeeze. Even here the number sits +52% above market — the puzzle §16 turns to.

_forces.intro:
The industry. Plasma-derived therapies is a near-unenterable oligopoly — CSL, Grifols, Takeda, Octapharma and Kedrion compete on supply reliability and yield rather than price, behind 5–10 year regulatory approvals and multi-billion-dollar fractionation capex. Secular immunoglobulin demand keeps the pool growing; the main constraint on industry profitability is payer-side price pressure as buyers consolidate. CSL spans three archetypes (plasma ~72%, vaccines, specialty pharma), so the rating is summarised across them.

Below, how CSL sits within that archetype, force by force — the company offsets are the Behring decomposition; Seqirus and Vifor sit at industry average.
rows: Payers (Medicare, EU health systems, hospitals) hold the purse, but the products are life-sustaining so volume is inelastic — the pressure is on price, with US Medicare Part D redesign the live front.
Same payer mix as peers; no CSL-specific pricing edge
Plasma is collected from paid US donors; supplier power is generally low but donor-collection labour is a real, cyclical cost lever exposed to US frontline wages.
Owns the largest plasma-donor collection network — vertical integration lowers input dependence
5–10yr FDA/EMA/TGA approval plus multi-billion fractionation capex make plasma near-unenterable; vaccines and specialty are low–moderate.
No CSL edge beyond the shared industry moat
No recombinant immunoglobulin at scale and biosimilar plasma is very hard; mRNA and gene therapy are a long-tail, industry-wide risk, not a near-term substitute.
Long-tail risk affects all fractionators equally
A rational oligopoly (CSL / Grifols / Takeda / Octapharma / Kedrion) competing on supply reliability and yield rather than price; capacity is added deliberately.
Scale leader → lower marginal cost via fractionation efficiency
_forces.net: +15 bps margin (supplier +5, rivalry-scale +10), 0 bps revenue growth. CSL captures the industry’s secular growth (Ig demand, indication expansion) plus a modest structural margin edge — but transmits macro stress through margin, not volume.

csl._position:
Businesses & moat
  • Three businesses on one balance sheet: CSL Behring (plasma-derived therapies, ~72% of revenue, ~42% margin), CSL Seqirus (influenza vaccines, ~14%, ~47% margin — demerger announced FY26), CSL Vifor (iron-deficiency / renal specialty pharma, ~14%, ~49% margin, acquired Aug 2022).
  • Franchise edge: the world’s largest plasma-collection network + fractionation scale + FDA/EMA/TGA barriers — a manufacturing / scale moat, not a patent moat (patent-cliff exposure very low).
Geography & demand
  • Geography / currency: global USD-functional group, ASX-listed AUD parent; US is ~55% of the plasma market. First worked example where the parent itself is USD-functional.
  • Demand character: price-inelastic in volume (life-sustaining Ig) — scenarios transmit through margin and policy, not volume.
Risks & capital
  • Key risk: US Medicare Part D redesign (~USD 100m Ig hit in 1H26) and China Ig/albumin access; donor-collection wage inflation is the other margin channel.
  • Capital: net debt ~1.8× EBITDA and de-levering; USD 750m buyback; Strategic Transformation targeting >USD 500m pre-tax savings by FY28.

The duplicated footprint is inflationary (~3.5%) and growth bifurcates — China-aligned economies may outpace the US-aligned bloc, with Europe hit hardest and Australia facing an acute security-vs-supply dilemma. The new equilibrium is structurally inferior.

Macro picture. Growth ~2.0%, below Muddle Through on supply-chain-duplication costs and bifurcated by bloc (China-aligned 3.5–4.0%; US-aligned ~1.8%). Advanced-economy inflation ~3.5%; real rates ~1.5%. USD reserve share erodes gradually but stays dominant; gold prominent as a cross-bloc settlement medium.

What would move the world elsewhere. Major diplomatic breakthroughs — a substantive US-China trade framework, a Russia-Ukraine settlement, an Iran deal revival — would weaken the bloc-formation logic; sustained globalisation gains in low-sensitivity categories would signal barrier-stability rather than ratcheting.
worldDesc.Disorderly Climate:
The already-running disorderly climate path has its crystallisation moment — most likely a confluence of a catastrophic insured-loss event, regulator-forced de-leveraging of carbon-intensive loan books, and a carbon-price spike. Policy snaps from drift to abrupt crisis action: carbon prices to EUR 200+, border-adjustment mechanisms, expanded transition subsidies. Capital reallocates abruptly, so sectoral dispersion widens sharply even as aggregate growth stays near Muddle Through (~2.0–2.2%, inflation 4.5–5% from carbon pass-through). This scenario tests terminal-state convergence hardest — assumed-perpetual moats reveal stranded-asset half-lives inside the horizon.

Macro picture. Aggregate growth 2.0–2.2% (near Muddle Through) but with far wider sectoral dispersion. Inflation peaks 4.5–5% from carbon-cost pass-through before easing to ~3% by year 10; real rates ~1.5% with elevated volatility. The EU ETS carbon price spikes to EUR 200+ and settles ~EUR 200–220; insurance is repriced sharply in physical-risk regions.

What would move the world elsewhere. Continued drift without crystallisation → Muddle Through; a political reset enabling orderly transition → Orderly Convergence; climate-policy backsliding under a macro crisis → Stagflation’s climate-stagnant posture.
worldDesc.AI Productivity Lag:
The Solow paradox at AI scale. Capability and capex advance genuinely (deficit-funded, US-led), but economy-wide productivity transformation doesn’t arrive on the bull timeline: enterprise adoption is slow, so aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5% versus the 1.5%+ current investment implies. Rents capture is asymmetric — platform owners take the bulk while broad enterprise pays without proportional payback — and market concentration intensifies. The saving grace is the labour-cost channel: AI contains white-collar wage growth even where productivity transmission is weak. Headline numbers resemble Muddle Through, but the underlying story differs.

Macro picture. Growth 1.9–2.0%, modestly below Muddle Through; inflation ~3.0% and real rates ~1.0% — both Muddle-Through-like. Aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5%. The tell: headline numbers resemble Muddle Through while the story underneath is fundamentally different.

What would move the world elsewhere. Enterprise-AI adoption broadening with genuine TFP flow-through → Orderly Convergence; an AI-capex collapse or financial-market unwind → a tech-investment-unwind stress variant outside the set; a major non-AI shock → Stagflation, Fragmentation or Disorderly Climate depending on the shock.

_drtheory: Risk-free rate

The theoretically correct rate is a zero-coupon (spot) sovereign yield in the cash-flow currency, matched to the timing of each cash flow — a coupon bond’s yield-to-maturity blends reinvestment assumptions across its life and is only an average. In practice the deep, liquid 10-year benchmark is used as a proxy, with longer tenors for very long-life assets; a steeply sloped curve is where that approximation most distorts long-dated NPVs.
10-year US Treasury, 4.50% (USD-functional). Single spot 10-year, matching CSL’s USD cash-flow currency — the correct-currency point behind rejecting the AUD-index beta below.
Equity risk premium

The expected excess return of equities over the risk-free asset. It is unobservable, so it is estimated from long-run historical premia, forward-looking/implied models, or surveys — none decisive. Mature-market estimates cluster around 5–6%, but the statistical error is wide, so the figure is best treated as a reasoned convention rather than a measurement.
5.0% — a Damodaran-style mature-market premium, ~100bps below the 6.0% Australian-expert convention.
Beta

A single-stock regression beta is noisy and shifts with the estimation window and the index chosen, so triangulate from a comparable set: unlever peer equity betas to asset betas and re-lever to the subject’s target capital structure, cross-checked against adjusted (mean-reverting) or fundamental betas. Index choice — local versus global — matters most when a company’s earnings currency differs from its listing.
Peer triangulation: Grifols / Takeda / Sanofi cluster 0.7–0.9 → selected 0.85. Measured 0.094 rejected — it regressed an AUD-listed price against an AUD index for a USD-earning business.
Cost of debt

The risk-free rate plus a credit-spread margin set by the company’s (or its comparable set’s) target credit rating, referencing traded corporate-bond spreads over sovereigns at matching tenor. Use a through-the-cycle target rating consistent with the assumed gearing, not the current coupon.
Not separately built — CSL’s DCF discounts FCFF at the cost of equity (8.75%) rather than a blended WACC; see ‘WACC vs cost of equity’ below.
Gearing / capital-structure weights

Weight equity and debt at market value on a target, through-the-cycle basis — informed by the subject’s own structure and the comparable-set average rather than a single spot snapshot, which is volatile and often inconsistent with the betas measured over the same window.
Not applied — the CSL DCF discounts FCFF at Re, so no debt/equity weighting is used.
WACC vs cost of equity

For an ordinary company, discount ungeared after-tax cash flows (FCFF) at the WACC and bridge enterprise value to equity via net debt. For a bank, funding — deposits and wholesale debt — is an operating input rather than financing, so discount cash flows to equity at the cost of equity directly; a WACC/EV bridge would be wrong.
A single cost of equity 8.75% is applied to FCFF rather than a blended WACC — a simplification worth flagging; it slightly understates the discount rate versus a formal WACC.
